one_liner: Unmaintained pure-Go cuckoo filter (Fan et al. 2014) offering deletion as a Bloom-filter alternative; speed claims unmeasured, known item-loss bugs.
what_it_does: A roughly 240-line Go package implementing the cuckoo filter, an approximate set-membership structure intended to replace a Bloom filter that can also delete items. The API is small and not Bloom-compatible: cfilter.New(opts...) takes functional options (Size in buckets, BucketSize, FingerprintSize in bytes, MaximumKicks, HashFn), and Insert/Lookup/Delete take []byte keys and return bool, with Count() alongside. With the defaults on master the filter has 65,536 buckets of 4 slots (262,144 fingerprints of 3 bytes). Insert returns false when the table is full. There is no constructor that sizes by capacity or target FPR, no serialization and no merge.
how_it_is_fast: It uses partial-key cuckoo hashing from Fan, Andersen and Kaminsky (CoNEXT 2014). Each key stores a short fingerprint (the leading bytes of its FNV-1 64 hash) in one of two 4-slot buckets, i1 = djb2(key) mod m and i2 = (i1 XOR djb2(fingerprint)) mod m. A lookup therefore reads at most two buckets instead of k scattered Bloom bits, and a delete just clears a slot. When both buckets are full, Insert evicts random fingerprints to their alternate bucket, up to 500 times. This Go implementation gives up most of the paper's cache-locality advantage: every slot is a 24-byte []byte slice header pointing at its own heap allocation, and every Insert/Lookup/Delete allocates twice (hash.Sum plus the fingerprint slice). Nothing in the repo measures the resulting speed.
when_to_use: Reading a short, clear Go walk-through of partial-key cuckoo hashing (insert, evict, XOR alternate bucket, delete) while learning the Fan et al. design.

Small, single-goroutine, throwaway sets of []byte keys that stay well below the 262,144-slot default capacity (the issue #13 reporter saw no losses at 200k keys but did at 300k), with Size left as a power of two, where an occasional false negative is acceptable.
Maintaining legacy code that already imports it (pkg.go.dev lists older OWASP Amass utils, finogeeks/ligase and osamingo/shamoji), where you need to understand its failure modes before replacing it.
when_not_to_use: Anything that relies on the usual no-false-negatives property. Users reported inserted items that later cannot be found: 5,162 of 100M keys in issue #11, and lookups failing past about 300k keys in issue #13. Both issues were closed without a fix, with the note 'No longer maintaining this' (2019-11-20).

Memory-sensitive use, which is the README's own headline claim. Each slot costs a 24-byte slice header whether it is used or not (about 7.5 MiB preallocated for the default 262k-slot filter), and each stored fingerprint is a separate heap allocation. At the default ~5e-7 FPR an optimal Bloom filter needs about 3.8 bytes per item (my arithmetic from the code and the paper's formula, not a measurement). A commenter in issue #13 estimated the footprint at 7x larger than necessary.
High load factors. The issue #11 reporter could not get past roughly 36-50% load before Insert failed, against the ~95% the paper reports for 4-slot buckets.
Concurrent access (no locking of any kind), persistence across restarts (the serialization request in issue #5 was closed unimplemented), or fingerprint sizes that are not a whole number of bytes.
Any setting where you want a maintained, tagged release. The last commit was 2017-07-05, and the only tags (v0.1.0 and v0.1.1, both 2016) predate every bug fix.

integration.dependencies: none (Go stdlib only: hash, hash/fnv, math/rand, bytes)
integration.min_toolchain: Not formally stated. There is no go.mod, and .travis.yml tested Go 1.3-1.6 plus tip in 2016-2017. Module mode resolves @latest to v0.1.1.
integration.platforms: any Go platform (pure Go, no unsafe or assembly)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented, and not safe. There is no mutex, and even Lookup mutates the filter's shared hash.Hash (Reset/Write/Sum), so concurrent read-only lookups race too. Insert and swap use the global math/rand.

gotchas: `go get github.com/irfansharif/cfilter` resolves to v0.1.1 (proxy.golang.org @latest), tagged 2016-09-11. That version still has the `i ^= hashfp(f) % cf.size` precedence bug, which panics with 'index out of range' once eviction starts (issue #8, fixed on master 2016-12-28), and a `rand.Intn(len(b)-1)` bug that never evicts the last slot (issue #10). panmari/compare_probabilistic_filters, which pins v0.1.1, commented cfilter out for exactly this panic. To get the fixes you must pin a master pseudo-version.

Even on master, the alternate-bucket XOR trick only round-trips when Size (the bucket count) is a power of two, which the default is. With any other Size, a fingerprint that gets evicted can land in a bucket Lookup never checks, so the filter returns false negatives. The losses reported in issue #11 used Size(20,000,000) and Size(35,000,000).

When Insert gives up after MaximumKicks, the fingerprint it is still holding is usually an earlier key's, and that key is silently dropped: Insert returns false, but Count() is not decremented and the lost key now fails Lookup. Insert also never checks for duplicates, so a key inserted twice is stored twice. Delete of a key that was never inserted can remove another key's matching fingerprint, as the README warns.

FingerprintSize is in bytes, not bits. Its doc comment says the default is 2, but master's configure() uses 3 bytes (v0.1.1 used 2), so the effective FPR, about 2*BucketSize/2^(8*bytes), depends on which version you got.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In practice, never for production. In Go, go-qfext (a quotient filter with measured 20-31 ns lookups against 74 ns for bits-and-blooms Bloom) or FastFilter/xorfilter (for static sets) are measured, working alternatives. efficient/cuckoofilter is the C++ reference whose paper numbers this README borrows. In 2017 the author himself pointed users to seiflotfy/cuckoofilter instead.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing was measured. The 'higher performance than Bloom filters' line restates the Fan et al. paper, whose figures come from the authors' C++ efficient/cuckoofilter. The repo's only benchmark inserts and deletes one constant key, with no Bloom baseline, no published results and no stated hardware. The only third-party numbers for cfilter (issue #11: 100M random 16-char hex keys, Go on an unspecified Mac, no Bloom comparison) show roughly 0.5M inserts/s and 1M lookups/s, with 5,162 inserted keys missing afterwards.
status_note: Abandoned. The last commit was 2017-07-05, and on 2019-11-20 the author closed all remaining issues with 'No longer maintaining this'. It is MIT-licensed, stdlib-only and about 240 lines, so it is easy to vendor, but the false-negative bugs above (power-of-two sizing, dropped eviction victim, stale v0.1.1 tag) would need fixing first.
